paragraphs.heading: Momentum for turning things
paragraphs.text: Angular momentum is the rotational partner of ordinary, or linear, momentum. It is also called moment of momentum or rotational momentum. It has both a size and a direction.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Angular momentum is conserved: when no net outside torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum stays constant. Torque can be defined as the rate at which angular momentum changes, much as force is for linear momentum. Both the size and the direction of the angular momentum are kept. Conservation narrows down how a system can move, though it does not settle the motion completely.

paragraphs.heading: How it is built
paragraphs.text: For motion in a line, momentum is mass times speed, p = mv. For a spinning object, angular momentum L is proportional to its moment of inertia I times its angular speed ω, measured in radians per second. Moment of inertia is unlike mass: it depends not only on how much matter there is but on where that matter sits relative to the axis of spin. For a single particle, angular momentum is r × p, combining its position r from a chosen origin with its momentum.

paragraphs.heading: It depends on the centre
paragraphs.text: Unlike linear momentum, angular momentum changes if you choose a different origin, because the particle's position is measured from that point. Strictly, then, L is the angular momentum about a particular centre. For a whole system, you add up the angular momenta of all its parts to get the total.

paragraphs.heading: Spin and orbit
paragraphs.text: There are two special kinds. Spin angular momentum is taken about an object's own centre of mass, and orbital angular momentum about some chosen centre of rotation. The Earth has both: orbital from circling the Sun, spin from turning on its polar axis each day. Its orbital share is about 2.66 × 10⁴⁰ J⋅s, while its spin share is about 7.05 × 10³³ J⋅s.

paragraphs.heading: Where you see it
paragraphs.text: Bicycles and motorcycles, flying discs, rifled bullets and gyroscopes all rely on conservation of angular momentum for their useful behaviour. The same rule is why hurricanes form spirals. It is also why neutron stars spin so fast.
